World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Live: Swans set for Magpies challenge while Suns tackle Power
World.content:
The ladder-leading Swans are at home to the Magpies while the Suns tackle the Power up north in a Friday night AFL double-header.

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

Live updates AFL Friday scoreboard D By Dean Bilton Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 14 Key Events 3 Swans vs Magpies 7 Highlights 1 Suns vs Power 2 All filters Collingwood kicks another H By Henry Hanson The Magpies continue their fast start. Chad Warner is expertly tackled in the centre of the field, the ball is arrowed into Lachie Shultz. He takes a mark and arrows through his set shot. Collingwood has the first two goals of the game and leads by 13 points. Solid stuff from Collingwood H By Henry Hanson We're over five minutes into the first quarter at the SCG, and so far so good for the Magpies. They've done well to squeeze the Swans in their defensive 50, have been full of energy and put up plenty of pressure. You can sense Sydney beginning to get a little tetchy as Brodie Grundy rises high but can't take a mark on the edge of his side's forward 50. Collingwood by seven points. West gets us underway H By Henry Hanson Charlie West takes a good mark wide on the left and just inside the 50. The second gamer makes good connection with the set shot and that's a great goal to put Collingwood seven points ahead. And we're off at the SCG! H By Henry Hanson As is traditional in the Marb Grook, the teams exchange gifts at the middle of the SCG. Collingwood gives a collection of handcrafted boomerangs made by James Collins, father of VFL player Hamish. And Sydney hands over a traditional fishing net made from bamboo. Lachie Schultz kicks the first behind of the game for Collingwood. The guernseys in question H By Henry Hanson Two brilliant strips on show at the SCG tonight, as we celebrate the excellence and contributions of First Nations people in the AFL. (Getty Images) Collingwood's is designed by 11-year-old Noongar Yamatji artist Jed Bennell and was inspired by the story of Magpies forward Bobby Hill. Loading Instagram content The Swans, meanwhile, are sporting an adaptation of a piece by renowned Bidiagal artist Jordan Ardler. Play is only moments away in Sydney Jamarra Ugle-Hagan a late out for Gold Coast D By Dean Bilton (AFL.com.au) Some big late news, with Ugle-Hagan out of the game with an ankle problem. He has been replaced by Jarrod Witts. That makes five changes overall for Gold Coast. Ethan Read, Ben Long, Ben Jepson and Alex Davies are also out, with Matt Rowell, Zeke Uwland, Nick Holman and Jed Walter coming in. Port are without Josh Lai, Miles Bergman and Jacob Wehr, replaced by Esava Ratugolea, Will Lorenz and debutant Tom Anastasopoulos. The ceremony begins at the SCG H By Henry Hanson The teams have entered the arena for the Marn Grook clash. Both teams are sporting special Sir Doug Nichols Round guernseys, and they're both looking lovely as we celebrate the excellence and the contribution of First Nations people in our great game. The Magun Zendath Kes Dance Group kicks us off with a performance, before Uncle Lloyd Walker conducts the Welcome to Country. The Gamay Dancers conclude the ceremony. Sydney vs Collingwood recent results H By Henry Hanson They're certainly underdogs tonight, but Collingwood got the job done over Sydney last year, triumphing by 31 points. In August 2024 the Swans won by three and in March that year, they won by 33. Sydney begins this game having won its last five games in 2026, while Collingwood has two wins, two losses, and of course, that ridiculous draw with Hawthorn two weeks ago. Can Collingwood contain Sydney's handball game? H By Henry Hanson (Getty Images) The Magpies have a massive test ahead of them in the Marn Grook clash at the SCG. The ladder-leading Swans have been fluid and slick through midfield all season, with their handball game being particularly impressive. The return of Charlie Curnow is also a big plus for the hosts, who will be hopeful of the first-year Swan freeing up Joel Amartey a touch, who had a quiet night in his absence last time out. Checking in from Darwin D By Dean Bilton (Getty Images) We're still a little over an hour away from this game, but the crowd is certainly starting to build at Marrara. (Getty Images) Port's 3-6 record doesn't make for great reading, but so many of those defeats have been by narrow margins. They may feel they are a better side than the ladder currently suggests. If so, this would be a fantastic night to prove it. 150 games for Rowbottom H By Henry Hanson A milestone night for Sydney midfielder James Rowbottom, who will play his 150th game for the club. The 25-year-old is building a very solid career for himself at the SCG. Outs for Collingwood, Curnow back for Sydney H By Henry Hanson (AFL.com) Scott Pendlebury is managed tonight and forced to wait for his record-breaking appearance, while Pies skipper Darcy Moore misses out after sustaining a concussion in last week's loss to Geelong. Patrick Lipinski and Darcy Cameron are also out injured, with Charlie West, Edward Allan, Will Parker and William Hayes coming in. It's good news for Sydney - Charlie Curnow is back, as is Jai Serong and Tom McCartin. World.title: Property developer bids $50,000 donation for lunch with deputy premier
World.content:
A developer has bid $50,000 for a lunch with Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, whose state government agency oversees land in which the developer has an interest.

The developer, David Trask, made the successful bid as a donation at lunch on Friday for the ruling Liberal National Party, held at the Brisbane Convention Centre and dubbed "Delivering for Queensland Industry Update".

The donation comes only two months after the LNP relaxed an eight-year ban on developers making contributions to political parties on a state level.

Mr Trask told the ABC on Friday that he has made donations to both sides of politics previously.

Do you know more? Contact Liam Walsh on encrypted email or Signal or Jack McKay on email.

He said the reality was that politicians were not the actual people who made decisions, and the state agency that oversees development would only make decisions in line with laws.

"The donations don't mean anything," he said.

"The donations [are] purely a goodwill gesture to a political party that runs our state, or our federal politics."

Plans and approvals have been active for development at North Harbour near Caboolture for decades, Mr Trask said, adding the that Labor Party had also been favourable previously to the project.

The North Harbour Priority Development Area is near Caboolture. (ABC News)

In May last year, the LNP declared part of the project to become a "priority development area" (PDA) under the purview of the powerful state agency Economic Development Queensland (EDQ), of which Mr Bleijie is the responsible minister.

A PDA is designed to speed up development and slash red tape. Mr Bleijie, at the time, flagged it would help build 3,700 new homes.

"While Labor tied up builders and councils in red tape, we're resetting the planning partnership with local councils and communities to deliver new housing," he said.

Some current flat scrubland in the area has been owned by Mr Trask's Trask Development Corporation for decades. Among ambitious plans is turning parts of North Harbour into an artificial marina with housing.

The final PDA is yet to be decided, with an interim plan in place. Mr Trask pointed out that Economic Development Queensland was still going through a series of studies associated with any development plan.

"It's my experience that it's not going to matter what I want," he said.

Mr Bleijie was listed as a keynote speaker at the "Delivering for Queensland Industry Update" on Friday, which was attended by mining-related figures and property developers.

The event on Friday was held at the Brisbane Convention and Exhibition Centre. (Brisbane Convention and Exhibition Centre)

The bidding at the lunch started at $5,000, Mr Trask said. He said multiple people made bids that increased in $500 increments.

Mr Trask believed the future event would be held at a restaurant.

"To be perfectly honest mate, I didn't read the detail," he said.

" A political donation is a political donation. I've had dinner with the [current] prime minister before. "

The donation laws were overturned, taking effect in March, after the LNP decried an earlier ban on developer donations as a financial gerrymander.

It often pointed the finger at the Labor Party, which brought in the state-level ban, while still being able to take money from unions.

A flyer for the fundraising lunch. (Supplied)

Mr Trask said he had a "fundamental issue with a government treating a tax-paying person like a criminal".

He said the earlier ban on developer donations was an example of one political party engaging in one-upmanship over another political party.

Mr Trask held out the prospect of donating to the Labor Party on a state level.

"That will depend on what their policy positions are at the time and if there's anything I see there of benefit to my business," he said.

Mr Bleijie's office on Friday referred to statements from Attorney General Deb Frecklington's office: "We've delivered on the position we took to the election to restore fairness and Queenslanders voted for it after they saw through Labor's disgraceful scare campaigns, which were bankrolled by the violent and misogynistic CFMEU."

EDQ told the ABC it operated within a state integrity framework so any conflicts of interest were identified and managed, and employees had to comply with codes of conduct.

"EDQ is not aware of any instance where a developer has attempted to link political donations to work involving EDQ," an agency spokeswoman said.

An LNP spokesperson said: "The Party strictly adheres to its compliance obligations."

World.title: 'Barbecue stopper' Asian tiger mosquito detected on Australian mainland for the first time
World.content:
The world's most invasive mosquito, known as the "barbecue stopper", has been detected for the first time on the Australian mainland.

Health authorities said six Asian tiger mosquitoes (Aedes albopictus) were found during routine surveillance near the Bamaga community, about 750 kilometres north-west of Cairns.

An aggressive daytime-biting insect, it can spread human viral diseases such as dengue and Japanese encephalitis.

Bamaga is a remote community 750km north-west of Cairns on the Cape York Peninsula in Far North Queensland. (Datawrapper: Conor Byrne)

Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service (TCHHS) said there was no threat to public health, but extensive spraying was underway on the Cape York Peninsula.

State MP for Cook David Kempton said while it is not considered an outbreak, the discovery was three males and three females.

"The biggest questions are, where are they coming from, and where are they now?" he said.

"If we find them in large numbers over a large area, we've certainly got an issue on our hands."

Thomas Schmidt is an expert in mosquitoes and genetics. (Supplied: Scimex)

University of Sydney Evolutionary Biology lecturer Tom Schmidt is an expert on the evolution of invasive insects.

He said the species excels at travelling with boats, planes, and trucks, and can survive cooler weather better than other tropical mosquitoes.

"I think this is the first time that they're seeing multiple individuals on the mainland and not at an airport or seaport," he said.

"It occasionally comes into Australian airports and seaports, and then those incursions will be eradicated."

He said it was "incredible" that the mosquito had only just been detected in the wild, 21 years after it was first found in the Torres Strait.

David Kempton is the LNP's Queensland state MP for Cook. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

'Barbecue stopper'

While the source of the incursion has not been confirmed, Mr Kempton said recent illegal foreign fisher incursions were a potential entry point.

"I couldn't discount that as a source," he said.

The female Aedes albopictus, also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. (Supplied QIMR: Chen Wu)

Dr Schmidt said genetic analysis could confirm where these particular insects originated from, and if that was connected to illegal foreign fishers.

"It seems that the original Torres Strait invasion around 2004-2005 was from an Indonesian source, which could have been fishermen," he said.

He said the "barbecue stopper" nickname referred to its aggressive nature.

"Aedes albopictus is known for biting repeatedly, and they're very painful bites," he said.

"When they're about, people tend to not want to go outside."

Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service acting executive director of medical services Ineke Wever. (Supplied: TCHHS)

No risk to public

TCHHS acting medical services director Ineke Wever said the detected mosquitoes did not carry any virus, but she urged residents to take precautions.

"The very best protection against mosquito-borne diseases is to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes in the first place,'' she said.

Dr Wever said wearing light-coloured, long-sleeved clothing, using insect repellents and screens, and regularly emptying water containers were good practices.

"All residents also need to do their part and take action to eliminate mosquito breeding sites on their properties and protect themselves from mosquito bites,'' she said.

World.title: Regional incinerator for Sydney waste draws unanimous ire at inquiry
World.content:
A NSW parliamentary inquiry in Goulburn has heard "universal non-support" for a proposed waste-to-energy plant at Tarago, with speakers questioning if existing environmental issues at the Woodlawn site undermine trust in the project.

The $600 million Veolia proposal would lead to about 380,000 tonnes of Sydney's non-recyclable waste burned each year at the company's existing Woodlawn site near Tarago, generating electricity for up to 40,000 homes.

The upper house Select Committee on Proposed Energy from Waste Facilities is conducting an inquiry into proposed energy-from-waste facilities in Tarago and Parkes.

Speaker after speaker told the inquiry they did not trust that the project would be safely operated, pointing to concerns linked to the Woodlawn landfill.

Resident Charlotte Payne said ongoing impacts had already affected her family.

"In the year-to-date, I've personally reported to the EPA over 40 occurrences of odour from the current operation at Veolia," she said.

" Such reports are only generated when the odour is so unbearable that it's causing significant distress to myself and my family and includes things like nausea, headaches and sleep disturbance. "

Calls for Sydney to keep its waste

Goulburn councillor Keith Smith asked why regional communities should host major waste infrastructure.

"If it's so safe, why don't we leave it in Sydney? We shouldn't be the dumping ground," he said.

Keith Smith tells the inquiry regional communities should not be asked to take Sydney’s waste. (Supplied: NSW Parliament)

Reverend Paul Davey, from St Nicholas' Anglican Church, said there was "no social licence" for the proposal.

"Our community stands united against waste incineration here or anywhere," he said.

" It is lazy government policy … and we are aghast that Sydney should propose to ban it for themselves but allow it here. "

Tuckerman rejects proposal

Goulburn MP Wendy Tuckerman said the proposal would shift long-term risks onto a small regional community.

"I believe that I am representing a majority of my constituents in my opposition," she said.

"The Tarago community is effectively being asked to accept long-term uncertainty that cannot be resolved within the life of monitoring or approvals."

Goulburn MP Wendy Tuckerman is concerned about environmental and community impacts. (Supplied: NSW Parliament)

During questioning, she acknowledged she was a cabinet minister when the former Coalition government's energy-from-waste framework was implemented, but said she had opposed the proposal and raised concerns with then-environment minister Matt Kean.

Shooters MP Mark Banasiak questioned her on a GIPA document she said showed Veolia sought changes to emissions standards, which she said "obviously diminishes" trust.

Stress and burnout

Local parent and farmer Thalia Sudumiano said she gave evidence because of "the pit I live with in my stomach" after hearing her property described as within a "death zone".

She said the project was making her children anxious.

"I brought them along for the fight. Whether or not that was a good idea, I will probably live with that for the rest of my life, but they are paying for it as well," she said.

Thalia Sudumiano says the proposal is deeply affecting her and her family. (Supplied: NSW Parliament)

Another Goulburn local, Andrew Wood, expressed similar despair.

"We stand at the 11th hour with time to stop this abomination," he said.

"Residents and landholders are already threadbare after years of uncertainty."

Farmers, including Stan Moore, detailed the concerns of primary producers.

"There is a risk to food safety … a risk that agricultural produce from contaminated areas will be banned from entering the food chain … and a risk to farmers' livelihoods should their land become contaminated," he said.

The Canberra Region Joint Organisation said energy-from-waste should remain a last resort, with greater focus on recycling.

After the hearing, Committee chair Nicole Overall said she was impacted by the "cumulative effect" on residents' mental health.

"What we saw today in the public hearing and yesterday in the public forum was definitely universal non-support for the proposal as it has been put forward," she said

Veolia defends proposal

In a statement, a Veolia spokesperson said the Woodlawn site was a complex former mine with extensive licensing conditions, and the company had prevented further environmental damage after taking over the insolvent operation 20 years ago.

It acknowledged odour issues and said it was working with the NSW EPA and independent experts on long-term solutions.

Veolia defended the proposal as internationally proven technology meeting best-practice standards.

"It is our hope that the same level of transparency and scrutiny applied to our proposal will also be applied to the claims made by others about pollution, emissions, agricultural impacts and health risks."

The inquiry will undertake further evidence-gathering before a final report is prepared.

World.title: WA treasurer concedes $217 million cost of racetrack project may blow out
World.content:
It will be difficult for the government to stick to the $217.5 million price tag to build a controversial new racetrack project in Perth, Western Australia's treasurer said, after assuring taxpayers for months the cost would not blow out.

But in a move that may have saved millions of dollars, the government has agreed to a no-money-exchanged land swap with the Crown Casino to purchase a crucial piece of land to build the track.

Artist impression of aerial view of Perth Park (Perth Entertainment and Sporting Precinct) in Burswood. (Supplied: WA government)

The project the government has dubbed Perth Park, after initially pitching it as a 'Motorsport Street Circuit' during the last election campaign, includes a 12,000-capacity outdoor amphitheatre, multi-purpose building and "multi-use racetrack" for cycling and an annual motorsport event.

Announcing a major building contract at the site on Friday, Treasurer Rita Saffioti said there was undoubted "pressure" to keep the budget in check.

Rita Saffioti speaks to reporters at the Burswood park site. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"Our ETCs [estimated total costs] is $217.5 [million], there's no doubt there's pressure on that budget, but we'll continue to target that number," she said.

" … there'll continue to be budget pressures as there are on all of our contracts."

"If there's changes to that ETC, then we'll make them at later dates but currently that's our estimated total cost.

"Like every project, there's always possibility of changes."

A view of the park's construction site. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Ms Saffioti also said a hospitality venue planned for inside the precinct will fall outside the $217.5 million budget given it wasn't "envisioned" as part of its original plan, though it's unclear how much that will cost.

Public backlash

Ms Saffioti had been steadfast for months the project's cost would not blow out — including when unveiling the state budget last week.

"Well, there's $217 [million] in the budget and that remains," she told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"That's our budget and that's what we're working towards."

Rita Saffioti, centre, speaks at the park site. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

Despite it being an election promise, there's been considerable public backlash from resident groups and a teaming up of Opposition and Greens disapproval.

Perth Park has had several names since its inception, but the government maintained all its elements had been clear from the start, including the many tweaks and changes made since it was first announced on the election campaign trail in January last year.

When asked whether the government is trying to bury the racetrack element, Ms Saffioti said "no".

"When we announced this, and I recall it very, very well … we announced that this is about the activation of the precinct," she said.

She said there was "always planning for an amphitheatre" which will benefit the arts and major events.

Roger Cook sat in a Supercar as the track proposal was announced. (Facebook: Roger Cook)

Zempilas digs in

Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas said the exclusion of the hospitality venue was an admission the $217.5 million price tag "cannot and will not be met".

"I don't believe this project is going to be delivered for the $217.5 million that the state government continues to suggest," he said.

"If they're separating this hospitality venue and now telling us it is a new element to this project, how could you claim that it's not part of the project if it's happening because of this redevelopment?"

WA Opposition leader Basil Zempilas spoke at a rally against the proposed racetrack development last year. (ABC News: Phoebe Pin)

Mr Zempilas also said current construction pressures would inevitably push the cost up.

"In this environment, it would be almost impossible to see how it didn't go up," he said.

"Why is it on this project in particular there is a determination from the state government not to give us clarity and certainty when it comes to what it is going to cost, what are they trying to hide?"

Land from Crown

The government had been in negotiations to own the land closest to the Crown Towers casino and resort complex as it was needed for the southern leg of the track.

The park will be located near the Crown Towers hotel complex. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Significantly, the government confirmed it had secured approximately 3.7 hectares of land from Crown worth over $36 million free-of-charge.

Burswood racetrack plan land woes Roger Cook may be planning victory laps around his controversial election-promised Burswood Park racetrack, but his government is being coy about one crucial element that could sink the whole thing.

Perth Park Steering Committee Chair, and Labor MP Daniel Pastorelli said the government had reached an "in principle agreement".

"As part of that land swap … Crown will receive approximately 1.85 hectares of land on the south-western corner of the existing Crown complex," he said.

Mr Pastorelli said the 3.7 hectares sold to Crown in 2013 was valued at $36.05 million and the 1.85 hectares the government was receiving in return was "independently valued and assessed" by Landgate at $16.9 million.

When asked if Crown was being short changed, Mr Pastorelli said there were many benefits in the deal.

Daniel Pastorelli speaks to the media. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"They are receiving land in a more strategic position for their future business operations … they already have private car parking in that vicinity, they will take over the car parking eventually as part of [the] land swap," he said.

World.title: Shoplifting is so bad in this town that police are homing in
World.content:
Victoria Police will crack down on aggressive shoplifters in Shepparton after thefts in the region hit a 10-year high.

A dedicated unit of five officers will begin daily patrols of Shepparton's shopping district on Sunday, targeting repeat offenders to prevent thefts and violence against shop staff.

Acting Superintendent Anna Parkinson said almost 800 offences were recorded in Greater Shepparton in 2025, and thieves were using intimidation and aggression towards retail staff to get away with their crimes.

A dedicated unit of five officers will begin daily patrols of Shepparton's shopping district. (ABC Shepparton: Charmaine Manuel )

"This is the first time in rural Victoria that an operation like this has been rolled out," she said.

" Under this operation, they [business owners] will have a direct link to this team in relation to the sharing of information that will allow us to act swiftly in order to identify these offenders. "

"Shepparton over the last few years has seen a substantial increase in retail crime," she said.

"But more alarming over the last 12 months, it's that escalation in behaviour of those offenders that has led us to have a dedicated team to deal with this type of offending."

Recent incidents in Shepparton include a 14-year-old girl who was charged with six offences after she allegedly threw glass objects at staff when confronted for stealing from a department store and chemist in February.

Police said the same teenager allegedly threw an open 1.25-litre bottle of soft drink at a staff member while leaving a supermarket in March.

Jac McCarty says some retail staff are scared to go to work. (ABC Shepparton: Charmaine Manuel )

A 32-year-old Shepparton man who allegedly stole more than $5,500 worth of electronics, a chainsaw, a bike, alcohol and groceries between March and May has been charged with 12 counts of shop theft and will face court next month.

Superintendent Parkinson said a similar program had been rolled out in Melbourne and had been "highly successful".

"There were a phenomenal amount of offenders that were held to account, and there was a lot of support provided to retailers, and a lot of intelligence gathered in relation to those operations that have led to significant arrests and results at court."

Retail staff scared to come into work

Greater Shepparton Business Network president Jac McCarty said retail crime is having a "major impact" around the Maude Street Mall and that staff were scared to come into work.

Ms McCarty owns a local retail shop in Shepparton and told ABC Radio Statewide Mornings yesterday that shoplifting was the main problem, but not the only one.

"There are [also] people, unfortunately, coming into stores and causing a little bit of havoc and people feeling unsafe, having to lock their doors," she said.

Australian Retail Council chief industry engagement officer Fleur Brown said, despite significant discussions with the Victorian government on retail crime, she is not satisfied with the response to date.

"We don't feel that that has been acted on with sufficient speed, and that is a real breaking point for a lot of retailers, so that is a top priority for us," she said.

"We'd like to see that support there."

The patrols will extend to Mooroopna and Tatura later this year.

World.title: Chloroform in drain suspected as reason hospital ward shut, staff ill
World.content:
An incident that prompted a Tasmanian hospital theatre to evacuate, and left several staff feeling ill, was possibly caused by chloroform, according to documents.

In September 2025, surgical staff at the Launceston General Hospital's theatre 4 reported feeling hot, faint, and nauseated.

The theatre was shut, except for essential staff who finished off a procedure, assisted by medical oxygen.

Three workers reported to the Emergency Department, and another worker later experienced adverse symptoms from home, all of whom have recovered.

According to a Tasmanian Health Service (THS) debriefing document, released under Tasmania's right-to-information laws, staff believed it could have been caused by chemical disposal in the neighbouring room.

According to RTI documents, it is hypothesised alcohol and chlorine were poured down the same sink, creating chloroform. (Unsplash: Alex Gorin)

"It is being hypothesised that 2 chemicals were poured into the sink in theatre 4's clean up room, alcohol and chlorine and created chloroform, and transferred to the theatre by the door being opened and closed a few times within a short time frame," the document said.

"With the way the HVAC (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning) units transfer air within the suites and provide fresh air every two minutes, there has been no way to confirm if this is the cause or not."

One of the documents noted that a staff member described a smell "like dry cleaning".

Chloroform was used as an anaesthetic in the 1800s.

It can be inhaled, absorbed through the skin, or ingested, and exposure to high levels can be fatal.

The THS engaged property, environment and safety consultant Prensa to conduct an indoor air quality assessment at the hospital, which found that disposing two chemicals — their names redacted — into the same drain with limited flushing was a "plausible" explanation.

A portion of the THS debriefing document, released under RTI. (Supplied)

"This hypothesis aligns with the specific symptoms reported by several staff on the day of the event," the report said.

"Airborne concentrations appear to have dissipated rapidly once the room was opened and ventilation/pressurisation restored — consistent with a short-lived, dense solvent-vapour plume dispersing rapidly under theatre air-change rates.

" A transient loss of positive pressure in the theatre (associated with clean-up room door access) may have facilitated the migration of this vapour plume from the clean-up room plumbing into the theatre. "

The report noted that while it could not determine the definitive source, other credible possibilities had been ruled out.

"The overall evidence is consistent with a credible but unverified transient solvent vapour exposure associated with operational room pressure dynamics, rather than a persistent HVAC or equipment fault," it said.

The incident occurred on the LGH's surgical ward. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The report made a series of recommendations, including stricter segregation of incompatible chemicals, improved trap management, and reinforcement of door and ventilation protocols, which it noted the hospital had implemented.

It also recommended that the THS investigate a neutralising product for chemical flushing and draining, develop procedures and checklists to ensure wastewater traps are primed regularly, repair dry traps and remove unused ones, and conduct regular checks to make sure theatres maintain positive pressure ventilation.

The health department has been contacted for comment.

During the investigation, Tasmania Fire Service tested airborne concentrations of oxygen, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, hydrogen disulphide, lower explosive limit, hydrogen cyanide and volatile organic compounds, but didn't detect any gases.

Other possible sources, like anaesthetic machines and surgical equipment, were also tested, but no faults were detected.

World.title: Boeing ordered to pay $69m to the family of woman killed in plane crash
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsAviation Boeing ordered to pay $69m to the family of woman killed in plane crash Rio Yamat May 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Chicago: A US jury has awarded $US49.5 million ($68.6 million) to the family of a 24-year-old global nonprofit worker killed in the 2019 crash of a Boeing 737 Max jet in Ethiopia while travelling to her first major assignment. The verdict, reached after a trial in federal court in Chicago, resolves one of the last remaining wrongful death lawsuits filed in connection with the disaster that killed all 157 people aboard Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. Samya Stumo, 24, was killed in the Ethiopian Airlines crash in 2019. Samya Stumo, who grew up in Sheffield, Massachusetts, had recently joined a nonprofit focused on strengthening health systems in developing countries. A 2015 graduate of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, she was travelling to Uganda for what would have been her first major project with the organisation when the plane crashed minutes after take-off from Addis Ababa on March 10, 2019. A spokesperson for UMass after the crash described her as someone known “for engaging others by earning their respect, friendship and trust.”



Jurors awarded $US21 million for the pain and suffering and emotional distress that Stumo experienced aboard the doomed flight, $US16.5 million for the loss of companionship suffered by her family and $US12 million for their grief, according to attorneys representing her estate. Related Article Aviation United Airlines jet just avoids ‘catastrophe’ after hitting a bakery truck and pole while landing “We are gratified for the opportunity to try the compensatory damages case,” attorneys Shanin Specter and Elizabeth Crawford said in a statement Wednesday evening announcing the verdict. It is the second verdict tied to the crash. Boeing has reached confidential pre-trial settlements in most of the dozens of wrongful death lawsuits filed in connection with the Ethiopian Airlines disaster and a similar 737 Max crash five months earlier off the coast of Indonesia that together killed 346 people. The fatal crashes became a defining crisis for Boeing and the 737 Max program. Investigators found that a flight-control system repeatedly forced the nose of the then-new planes downward based on faulty readings from a single sensor, and pilots in both crashes were unable to regain control.



The verdict follows a November 2025 jury award of $US28.45 million to the family of Shikha Garg, a United Nations environmental consultant who also died in the 2019 crash. That case marked the first civil jury trial stemming from the disaster, with jurors similarly tasked only with calculating damages because Boeing has accepted liability. “We are deeply sorry to all who lost loved ones on Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. While we have resolved nearly all of these claims through settlements, families are entitled to pursue their claims through the court process, and we respect their right to do so,” a Boeing spokesperson said on Thursday in a statement. Stumo was travelling to Uganda for what would have been her first major project with the organisation when the plane crashed minutes after take-off from Addis Ababa in 2019. AP The Ethiopian Airlines crash prompted a worldwide grounding of the 737 Max that lasted more than a year and triggered multiple investigations into Boeing’s safety culture and regulatory oversight. Federal prosecutors later charged Boeing with misleading regulators about the Max’s flight-control system, though in November, the federal judge in Texas overseeing the long-running criminal case approved a Justice Department request to dismiss it. Prosecutors reached an agreement with Boeing, requiring the company to invest an additional $US1 billion in fines, family compensation and safety improvements.

World.title: Scott Morrison, slimmed-down man for all seasons, gets a new platform
World.content:
Perspective NationalScott Morrison Scott Morrison, slimmed-down man for all seasons, gets a new platform Tony Wright May 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scott Morrison is a man of many parts, as anyone might know who remembers his startling secret acquisition of a string of portfolios to add to his job of prime minister during the COVID lockdown years. Now he has a new image altogether to add to his curriculum vitae. The unveiling of Scott Morrison’s bronze bust in Ballarat. Ruby Alexander He is the latest of 30 former prime ministers to be memorialised with a sculptured bust in Ballarat’s Avenue of Australian Prime Ministers. The bronze bust, created after a series of careful measurements during sittings with sculptor Martin Moore in the end days of Morrison’s political career several years ago, betrays changes wrought by time.



It presents the fleshy face of a man who had enjoyed years of prime ministerial dining, long hours at a desk and travelling in the comfort of chauffeur-driven cars and VIP jets. “I’ve shed a few pounds since back then,” conceded the former prime minister, peering at the image that will forever sit on a pedestal in the avenue of political leaders that stretches through old Ballarat’s gardens on the shore of Lake Wendouree. Scott Morrison comes face-to-face with the bronze bust at Friday’s ceremony. Ruby Alexander “I’ve had a bit more time to sort of have a bit more exercise [post politics].” Indeed, Morrison, who travels the world these days meeting the demands of a series of international consultancies and pushing the attributes of the AUKUS nuclear submarine deal that he squired as prime minister, has transformed into a trim, slim fellow in a much better-fitting suit than those he once wore.



He declared himself humbled to be part of what he described “a magnificent tradition here in Ballarat” – the only avenue in Australia of the sculptured busts of every prime minister since federation. He reflected at some depth on part of his own political career, speaking of the isolating challenges he faced during the pandemic, and musing about the unpopularity attached to leadership under pressure. Former PM John Howard, he said, had advised him that “there is no ideology in a crisis, there is just fixing it and seeing your country through; you put everything else aside, politics no longer means anything to you”. Morrison drew a curious parallel with one of his unlikely political heroes, Joe Lyons, a Labor minister until he quit the ALP during the Great Depression of the early 1930s, joined the United Australia Party and became prime minister. Lyons was ever after considered a “rat” by Labor, but Morrison said he steered Australia away from 25 per cent unemployment and began to rebuild the nation’s economic foundations.



“I wanted to tell that story about Joe Lyons today because, like him and many others who stand behind me [in the avenue of prime ministers], they were not always loved. “Often they were loved and unloved over the course of their administration; I have some sense of that. Scott Morrison and his family take a selfie to commemorate the moment. Ruby Alexander “Very few political stories end well.” It sounded as close to an exposure of Morrison’s inner turmoil concerning his turbulent prime ministership as you are likely to hear from him.



Indeed, the avenue of prime ministers had a moment a few years ago that spoke comically of his unpopularity in some quarters. In 2022, sculptor Louise Pratt and activist Rob Beamish created a bust of Morrison and hoisted it to a pedestal on Ballarat’s celebrated avenue. The satirical version that was created in 2022 and ended up in Ballarat’s art gallery. It was created from coal-impregnated resin, satirising Morrison’s production in parliament of a lump of coal to reinforce his argument that coal should not be demonised in the debate about climate change. The activists’ effort was swiftly removed from the avenue. But the Ballarat Art Gallery purchased it, ensuring it would continue to be a reminder of a climate of controversy during Morrison’s leadership.



Related Article King’s Birthday Honours Politicians, scientists and costume designer feature in King’s awards It’s not every former prime minister who has two sculpted busts in Ballarat, he might reflect, though no one spoke of it when he came to the shore of Lake Wendouree on Friday. He wasn’t prepared to speak about the current political turmoil for the Liberal-Nationals Coalition in Canberra, either. “I’ll leave those things to the politicians who are still serving,” the former PM said. As to whether he has been asked by his former colleagues for advice about what to do in the emergency, Morrison wasn’t about to break his self-imposed code of silence.



“One of the things I pledge to my colleagues, which I’ve honoured, is that any advice I give them I give to them privately and personally.” He allowed that “it’s a challenging time for all of them, but I really commend Angus for what he had to say on Thursday night [in his budget reply].” A glimpse of the former Liberal politician came through when he added: “I think he [Angus Taylor] set out a very comprehensive alternative to how Australia needs to face the very serious challenges that are ahead of us, and I think that Angus’ invitation to ‘believe again’ was a good one, and it’s certainly one that I share a belief in.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Boldness is in the air
World.content:
NationalNSWNote From The Editor Boldness is in the air Jordan Baker May 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A budget lock-up is a strange event, involving hours of wading through budget papers, conferring with colleagues and racing towards a 7.30pm deadline, powered by a smorgasbord of snacks. There’s no internet or smartphones; the Sydney team chatted with our Canberra friends on a phone with a handset. For those of us old enough to remember life without the constant ping of mobile phone messages, it felt pleasantly early ’90s. Treasurer Jim Chalmers delivers his budget address. Alex Ellinghausen The amount of organisation that goes into a budget lock-up is enormous. A team of at least 50 tech, administration, support and editorial production staff began meeting in December to plan and test for budget day. Our systems and technologies for both print and the website have to be reconfigured to operate entirely offline, to adhere to the Treasury’s strict confidentiality rules. All for the six-hour window from when the budget papers are released until the treasurer starts his speech. It’s a huge, complex undertaking, and it runs smoothly thanks to the incredible work of our production guru Michael Gadd, our Canberra bureau chief Michelle Griffin, and our national content director Chris Paine. Every year, as the embargo lifts, readers rush to the Herald‘s website for the opinions of our experts, such as economics editor Ross Gittins and political editor Peter Hartcher, and to read the analysis and news from our political and economics writers. They always love the illustrations on the front page – this year’s cracker, by Cathy Wilcox, was a lighthearted rendering of Treasurer Jim Chalmers bursting the Boomers’ bubble.



Bursting the Boomers’ bubble. Cathy Wilcox Often, though, budgets can be incremental and prosaic. This one wasn’t. The Labor government’s decision to reform negative gearing, capital gains tax and trusts was enormously consequential for many Australians, who suddenly had to re-think their investment strategies. Readers can get a quick summary of the budget in our five-minute version, or in this video of Gittins and economics writer Millie Muroi answering readers’ questions. Reader responses to the budget were varied. Some were angered by the government’s decision to break its pre-election undertaking to steer clear of CGT and negative gearing, and they felt the reforms were unfair. Others reckoned there was merit in the argument that circumstances – such as the housing affordability crisis – demand bold action, and that Australia’s failure over many electoral cycles to attempt such boldness is holding the country back. On budget night, the Herald endorsed Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ decision to overhaul taxes on investment in the hope that a reshaping of property market dynamics will pave the way for more young Australians to buy a home, but we pointed out there’s more to be done. Boldness, it appears, is in the air. In his budget reply on Thursday night, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor pledged to end bracket creep and to index tax brackets to inflation, another big – albeit expensive – reform that many economists think is long overdue. As Hartcher will write in his column tomorrow, Australia has not seen such reform ambition for 25 years, since John Howard introduced the goods and services tax.

Upstairs, the master bedroom’s en suite features a skylit circular bath, while downstairs, the custom wine cellar and underfloor heating in both bathrooms add a sense of luxury. 35 Cecily Street, Lilyfield, NSW This 1920s Californian bungalow has been given a new lease on life.

Designed with function and flow, the ground floor includes zoned living, while the main and secondary bedrooms are upstairs. Outside is an all-weather entertainer’s terrace with an integrated barbecue, a landscaped garden, and a mosaic-tiled pool with an outdoor heated shower.

Port Adelaide coach Josh Carr has detailed how he and Port Adelaide have handled the decision facing Zak Butters on whether he returns to Victoria, reiterating the hard line on compensation that the club will take if their champion and free agent chooses to leave. Carr said the Butters discussion, one of the major AFL stories of 2026, had not impacted on team performance, and that he and Butters had been “really open with each other” about his situation. Port Adelaide coach says his lines of communication with star playmaker Zak Butters are open as the Victorian considers his options as a free agent. AFL Photos via Getty Images Carr also made a strong case for the AFL to amend a problem in the bidding system rule change, highlighting the problem facing not just Port Adelaide but potentially any of the 18 clubs in 2027 when Tasmania will have the lion’s share of the first round of the national draft. While Butters is exploring a move back to Victoria – with the Bulldogs and Geelong viewed as frontrunners for him – the Port Adelaide coach said the club had achieved a scenario in which Butters and the Power had put the team first, without affecting team performance this year.



“I’ve been there myself as a player,” Carr told this masthead in an exclusive interview before the Power’s game in Darwin, speaking of Butters. Carr navigated a trade to Fremantle after Port won the 2004 premiership. Related Article AFL 2026 Fines, votes and free agency: None of it seems to distract Zak Butters “I think everyone understands when a player comes out of contract, they’ve got every right to explore and understand what’s out there. “And we understand that players do want to go home, and we want to bring players back to Adelaide that are from Adelaide.” Carr indicated, too, that Port retained an interest in Saints star Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera if he explored a move, the Saints gun having signed only a two-year extension last year.



“So to understand the landscape, I think the maturity of us as a footy club, but also Zak himself, is about now and about our investment in the football club right now, and making sure we’re all getting better. “And he’s a great leader of our footy club. He leads by example. He demands high standards around the footy club, and that hasn’t stopped, and so we’ve been really honest with each other about what that looks like, and about making sure we put the team first, and, and that’s been the goal for everyone, and feel like that’s being achieved right now. Port Adelaide have made a competitive start in Josh Carr’s maiden season as senior coach. AFL Photos via Getty Images “We’re always really, really open with each other and what it looks like. But again, what it ends up coming back to is making sure the team isn’t being affected. And I don’t think it is.” The Power have been highly competitive in Carr’s maiden season as senior coach, toppling Geelong and almost beating Hawthorn.



He is unequivocal the club will match any offer for Butters if the player exercises his free agency rights, which would then force a trade. Butters would fetch just one first round choice for the Power if they let simply leave, but in a trade Port will demand far more. “It’s not even really a discussion … we will match it. So whatever it is, it’ll be matched,” Carr said. Loading Like Carlton, Port has rights to a potential No.1 pick in this year’s this draft – academy recruit Doug Cochrane. But Carr said the Power were not thinking of Cochrane – who could cost the draft equivalent to picks four and eight if a bid was made for him at No.1 – as an effective swap for Butters. “We’re not really thinking about it like that,” he said.



Speaking on the Tasmania’s impact on draft bids in 2027 – when the Power will have the rights to take highly rated youngster Louis Salopek as a father-son selection and potentially another recruit from their next-generation academy – Carr said the AFL needed to consider all clubs, not simply the Devils, with its 2027 draft rules. Related Article Tasmania Devils ‘Our mainland cousins are feeling the heat’: Tassie stadium cost makes clubs nervy The league has made the price higher for clubs with rights to father-son and academy players, with two picks the maximum that can be used to match a bid under the revised system. Port’s position is not to oppose Tasmania’s draft haul, which will include picks 1,3, 5, 7, 9 and more. They want the bid to be in line with ladder position, and their “natural” pick rather than the skewed order created by Tasmania owning the lion’s share of the early part of the draft. If the AFL uses the actual 2027 picks – irrespective of ladder order – clubs will find it harder to match bids.



“From my point of view as a coach, we do everything we can to get those players, and we will, and there’s still a bit to go with what next year looks like with Tasmania coming in,” he said. “We just hope the AFL are thinking about everyone, we’re not just Tasmania when it comes to those decisions. “So right now, if it keeps going like it is, the value of our pick could slide off on the back of what Tasmania have. “So there’s conversations being had, and we hope it comes into consideration that, you know, whoever it is – it’s not just us – it is all AFL clubs, that if you have a pick, that value holds with the bids that come in from Tassie.” Carr said Port tried hard to lure Wanganeen-Milera last year and retained an interest if he was open to a move.



“I don’t need to go into details as far as me and that, but to say that I put a lot of work in, like every club, to get the best players in the competition,” he said. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL LIVE: Swans overwhelmed by Magpies’ pressure early; star forward a late out of Friday night footy “He was one it would have been nice to ... get him over to, or back to, Adelaide. But that’s the way it was. “We want good players. Want to bring the players back to Adelaide, and if he’s open to a move, then we’ll be having those conversations.” Carr said gun midfielder Jason Horne-Francis, the No.1 draft pick of 2021, had matured in how he prepared for the AFL, agreeing with those who likened the powerful matchwinner to Hawthorn’s Luke Hodge, who took time to become a superstar in comparison to West Coast’s Chris Judd when they both emerged from the 2001 draft.



“I think if you look at the way he’s prepared himself now, like physically, he looks elite now; the way he looks after his body and his understanding of what it takes to be a professional footballer. He’s got so much upside. “I think that’s fair (comparison). He loves football, but he loves his mates as well. ” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

It was March 2023, and Sydney Sweeney was holding court in the Swans rooms. Her first visit to the SCG had coincided with a home win over Hawthorn, and the presence of one of Hollywood’s hottest actors took the post-match celebrations to another level.

Not everybody, however, received the memo. Amid the buzz of this star-struck meet-and-greet, John Longmire quietly approached a member of club staff and asked: “Who is this person?”

Sydney Sweeney first visited the Swans in 2023 when filming in the Harbour City. Instagram

Said staff member asked the then head coach if he had seen the television series Euphoria, which drew a blank look. He could comfortably identify Rachel Griffiths, who was also there alongside co-star Dermot Mulroney, though you suspect he might have been more familiar with Muriel’s Wedding than Anyone But You – the rom-com the trio were in Sydney to film.

But then, what is a generational disconnect if not an observational moment? A chance to acknowledge that sport is for all ages, interests and orientations. And that the Sydney Swans seem to have a knack of catering for each at the same time. Longmire graciously introduced himself to Sweeney in the pleasant, unaffected manner that was symbolic of the rusted-on Swans supporters who’d attended the game solely for the footy.

World.title: ‘I probably don’t want to leave’: Trump gushes over China during tiptoe among the trees
World.content:
Beijing: As Chinese leader Xi Jinping took his US rival on a stroll through the secretive compound of the Communist Party, he pointed out the historic trees that have flourished since imperial times. “Let me tell you, all the trees here are over two or three hundred years old, and there’s another tree over 400 years old over there,” Xi told US President Donald Trump through an interpreter as they wandered the gardens of Zhongnanhai. Xi Jinping takes Donald Trump on a tour of the historic trees that have flourished since imperial times. Getty Images The symbolism of the old trees taps the cornerstone theme Beijing likes to project. Getty “There are also 1000-year-old trees in other places.”



It was one of several highly choreographed glimpses of the Xi-Trump dynamic that the press was invited to record across the two-day summit, which featured hours of closed-door negotiations over the thorny issues of trade, Taiwan, the Iran war and artificial intelligence. The symbolism of the old trees taps the cornerstone theme Beijing likes to project. China has endured for thousands of years – a measure by which the American empire is a recent phenomenon, and one Xi believes is in decline. Loading If Trump picked up on the messaging, he gave little away, keeping himself on an uncharacteristically tight leash with his public remarks throughout the summit. “Nice, nice place. I like it. I like this place. I can get used to staying here, and I probably don’t want to leave,” he told Xi, as they lingered in the gardens.



For a summit low on expectations but high on optics, Xi delivered a carefully crafted spectacle designed to project China’s status as the foremost peer to the US, occupying the rarefied air of two superpower nations capable of reshaping international relations for better or worse. The “China-US relationship is the most important bilateral relationship in the world. We must make it work and never mess it up”, Xi said in a toast, as the Chinese side hosted Trump at a banquet at The Great Hall of the People on Thursday evening. Trump and Xi arriving for Thursday’s state banquet in the Great Hall. Getty Images The table setting for the banquet. Getty Images These kinds of highly billed proceedings rarely land consequential outcomes themselves or change the fundamentals of bilateral relationships, and they are designed as much to send messages to their domestic audiences as they are to the world.



“This is a boxing match between two very good heavyweights,” says Dennis Wilder, a former White House intelligence official who helped arrange then-president George W. Bush’s trips to China. “They’re both great at this game. Both leaders are quite confident that they own the high ground.” Xi delivered a carefully crafted spectacle designed to project China’s status as the foremost peer to the US. Getty Images Asked if he was enjoying his visit, Trump responded with a thumbs-up. Xi has not taken a question from the press since 2017. Getty Images As the two men strolled through Zhongnanhai, a travelling US reporter was cut off by Chinese minders for trying to lob a question.



“No questions,” the reporter was told when he asked Trump if he was enjoying his visit. Trump responded with a thumbs-up. Xi has not taken a question from the press since 2017. Related Article China relations Trump wraps up Beijing summit with plenty of goodwill but few blockbuster deals The incident serves as a reminder of the fundamental ideological differences between the two nations – one obsessed with individual freedom and the other with control; one run by a president whose volubility knows few constraints and the other by a leader who never goes off script. After a turbulent year in which Trump kicked off his second-term presidency with a tariff war, from which Xi refused to back down, the US-China relationship found a fragile truce in October when the pair met on the sidelines of the APEC summit in South Korea. Since then, China experts have debated whether the leverage has shifted in Xi’s favour as Trump arrived in Beijing this week with the economic damage of the Iran war hammering his popularity at home, and his tariff regime crippled by the US courts.



For his part, Xi unveiled a new framing for the China-US relationship as one based on “constructive strategic stability”, which state media said was meant to “provide strategic guidance for the next three years and beyond”. In the tepid language of Communist Party speak, it may sound underwhelming, but China analysts will spend considerable time unpacking it as Beijing rarely throws out new declarative statements. Xi also packaged it with a well-worn warning on Taiwan – that this stability hinged on the US not “mishandling” the reddest of all red lines for China. The Trump administration remains confident that the trip by the US president will deliver results. Getty Images “This tells us two things: that US-China relations are stable, but also they are not partners, because they still do not align on matters of fundamental strategic interest,” says Wen-Ti Sung, a Taipei-based specialist on China-Taiwan relations at the Australian National University. To Americans, China came across in this summit as economically permissive but politically hardball. George Chen, a partner at The Asia Group consultancy, said Xi’s remarks drew clear boundaries for the US while offering reassurance to American businesses.



“Politically, the message was unequivocal: everything begins with Taiwan,” he said. “Xi expressed zero tolerance for any moves toward Taiwan independence, and he placed this ‘red line’ at the very start of his meeting with Trump. There was no ambiguity, no softening – just a direct restatement of China’s core position.” Trump signed off on a $US11 billion ($15 billion) arms package to Taiwan last year, infuriating China, which regards the island democracy as its own territory. A further $US14 billion in weapon sales is awaiting Trump’s approval, and Xi was expected to press him to delay or withhold it during their summit talks. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said America’s Taiwan policy remained “unchanged” in an interview with NBC from the sidelines of the summit. “They always raise it on their side. We always make clear our position, and we move on to the other topics,” said Rubio, who was among senior aides to join Trump for the talks.



Xi’s directive of “constructive strategic stability” will now filter down through the byzantine network of the Communist Party system. “Once the signal from Xi himself comes out, that’s actually the directive to the working level officials on how they need to proceed with their relationship with the US counterparts,” says Dylan Loh, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Summits such as this are designed as much to send messages to the domestic audience as they are to the world. Getty Images “It’s a signal to the entire ecosystem that we are looking for stability … not confrontation.” Trump, eager to announce “wins”, said the two men had made “some fantastic trade deals”, as he touted his strong relationship with Xi in a message also aimed at shoring up stability.



“We’ve settled a lot of different problems that other people wouldn’t have been able to settle. And the relationship is a very strong one. We’ve really done wonderful things, I believe,” he said in brief remarks before the press at Zhongnanhai. With the details of the summit still yet to filter into the public domain, some of the more concrete substance about the leaders’ apparent discussions has come through Trump’s interviews with Fox News while in Beijing. He said China had agreed to buy 200 Boeing jets and that Xi had offered to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz, claims the Chinese side has not commented on. To Americans, China came across in this summit as economically permissive but politically hardball. AP “He did offer. He said, ‘If I can be of any help at all, I would like to be of help’,” Trump told Fox’s Sean Hannity, recounting his conversation with Xi. The Iran war has added a fresh source of tension to the US-China relationship due to the fact that Beijing is Tehran’s chief financial backer as the major buyer of its oil. But experts have been sceptical that Beijing has any meaningful influence over Tehran, or that it would be willing to leverage it to help the US resolve a war of its own making.



By the time the wheels were up on Air Force One out of Beijing, it was not clear if Trump had secured any firm commitments from Xi on Iran, or what he might have traded to get a deal for Chinese support. By the time the wheels were up on Air Force One out of Beijing, it was not clear if Trump had secured any firm commitments from Xi on Iran, or what he might have traded to get a deal for Chinese support. AP The stage is set, however, for a year of summitry between the world’s two most powerful men. Trump invited Xi to the White House in September, and he could return to China in November for APEC in Shenzhen, the country’s tech capital. Plenty of opportunity for the leaders to hone their optics, while the furious competition between their countries for prestige and power on the world stage remains unchanged. World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsAviation Boeing ordered to pay $69m to the family of woman killed in plane crash Rio Yamat May 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Chicago: A US jury has awarded $US49.5 million ($68.6 million) to the family of a 24-year-old global nonprofit worker killed in the 2019 crash of a Boeing 737 Max jet in Ethiopia while travelling to her first major assignment. The verdict, reached after a trial in federal court in Chicago, resolves one of the last remaining wrongful death lawsuits filed in connection with the disaster that killed all 157 people aboard Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. Samya Stumo, 24, was killed in the Ethiopian Airlines crash in 2019. Samya Stumo, who grew up in Sheffield, Massachusetts, had recently joined a nonprofit focused on strengthening health systems in developing countries. A 2015 graduate of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, she was travelling to Uganda for what would have been her first major project with the organisation when the plane crashed minutes after take-off from Addis Ababa on March 10, 2019. A spokesperson for UMass after the crash described her as someone known “for engaging others by earning their respect, friendship and trust.”



Jurors awarded $US21 million for the pain and suffering and emotional distress that Stumo experienced aboard the doomed flight, $US16.5 million for the loss of companionship suffered by her family and $US12 million for their grief, according to attorneys representing her estate. Related Article Aviation United Airlines jet just avoids ‘catastrophe’ after hitting a bakery truck and pole while landing “We are gratified for the opportunity to try the compensatory damages case,” attorneys Shanin Specter and Elizabeth Crawford said in a statement Wednesday evening announcing the verdict. It is the second verdict tied to the crash. Boeing has reached confidential pre-trial settlements in most of the dozens of wrongful death lawsuits filed in connection with the Ethiopian Airlines disaster and a similar 737 Max crash five months earlier off the coast of Indonesia that together killed 346 people. The fatal crashes became a defining crisis for Boeing and the 737 Max program. Investigators found that a flight-control system repeatedly forced the nose of the then-new planes downward based on faulty readings from a single sensor, and pilots in both crashes were unable to regain control.



The verdict follows a November 2025 jury award of $US28.45 million to the family of Shikha Garg, a United Nations environmental consultant who also died in the 2019 crash. That case marked the first civil jury trial stemming from the disaster, with jurors similarly tasked only with calculating damages because Boeing has accepted liability. “We are deeply sorry to all who lost loved ones on Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. While we have resolved nearly all of these claims through settlements, families are entitled to pursue their claims through the court process, and we respect their right to do so,” a Boeing spokesperson said on Thursday in a statement. Stumo was travelling to Uganda for what would have been her first major project with the organisation when the plane crashed minutes after take-off from Addis Ababa in 2019. AP The Ethiopian Airlines crash prompted a worldwide grounding of the 737 Max that lasted more than a year and triggered multiple investigations into Boeing’s safety culture and regulatory oversight. Federal prosecutors later charged Boeing with misleading regulators about the Max’s flight-control system, though in November, the federal judge in Texas overseeing the long-running criminal case approved a Justice Department request to dismiss it. Prosecutors reached an agreement with Boeing, requiring the company to invest an additional $US1 billion in fines, family compensation and safety improvements.

World.title: Scott Morrison, slimmed-down man for all seasons, gets a new platform
World.content:
Perspective NationalScott Morrison Scott Morrison, slimmed-down man for all seasons, gets a new platform Tony Wright May 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scott Morrison is a man of many parts, as anyone might know who remembers his startling secret acquisition of a string of portfolios to add to his job of prime minister during the COVID lockdown years. Now he has a new image altogether to add to his curriculum vitae. The unveiling of Scott Morrison’s bronze bust in Ballarat. Ruby Alexander He is the latest of 30 former prime ministers to be memorialised with a sculptured bust in Ballarat’s Avenue of Australian Prime Ministers. The bronze bust, created after a series of careful measurements during sittings with sculptor Martin Moore in the end days of Morrison’s political career several years ago, betrays changes wrought by time.



It presents the fleshy face of a man who had enjoyed years of prime ministerial dining, long hours at a desk and travelling in the comfort of chauffeur-driven cars and VIP jets. “I’ve shed a few pounds since back then,” conceded the former prime minister, peering at the image that will forever sit on a pedestal in the avenue of political leaders that stretches through old Ballarat’s gardens on the shore of Lake Wendouree. Scott Morrison comes face-to-face with the bronze bust at Friday’s ceremony. Ruby Alexander “I’ve had a bit more time to sort of have a bit more exercise [post politics].” Indeed, Morrison, who travels the world these days meeting the demands of a series of international consultancies and pushing the attributes of the AUKUS nuclear submarine deal that he squired as prime minister, has transformed into a trim, slim fellow in a much better-fitting suit than those he once wore.



He declared himself humbled to be part of what he described “a magnificent tradition here in Ballarat” – the only avenue in Australia of the sculptured busts of every prime minister since federation. He reflected at some depth on part of his own political career, speaking of the isolating challenges he faced during the pandemic, and musing about the unpopularity attached to leadership under pressure. Former PM John Howard, he said, had advised him that “there is no ideology in a crisis, there is just fixing it and seeing your country through; you put everything else aside, politics no longer means anything to you”. Morrison drew a curious parallel with one of his unlikely political heroes, Joe Lyons, a Labor minister until he quit the ALP during the Great Depression of the early 1930s, joined the United Australia Party and became prime minister. Lyons was ever after considered a “rat” by Labor, but Morrison said he steered Australia away from 25 per cent unemployment and began to rebuild the nation’s economic foundations.



“I wanted to tell that story about Joe Lyons today because, like him and many others who stand behind me [in the avenue of prime ministers], they were not always loved. “Often they were loved and unloved over the course of their administration; I have some sense of that. Scott Morrison and his family take a selfie to commemorate the moment. Ruby Alexander “Very few political stories end well.” It sounded as close to an exposure of Morrison’s inner turmoil concerning his turbulent prime ministership as you are likely to hear from him.



Indeed, the avenue of prime ministers had a moment a few years ago that spoke comically of his unpopularity in some quarters. In 2022, sculptor Louise Pratt and activist Rob Beamish created a bust of Morrison and hoisted it to a pedestal on Ballarat’s celebrated avenue. The satirical version that was created in 2022 and ended up in Ballarat’s art gallery. It was created from coal-impregnated resin, satirising Morrison’s production in parliament of a lump of coal to reinforce his argument that coal should not be demonised in the debate about climate change. The activists’ effort was swiftly removed from the avenue. But the Ballarat Art Gallery purchased it, ensuring it would continue to be a reminder of a climate of controversy during Morrison’s leadership.



Related Article King’s Birthday Honours Politicians, scientists and costume designer feature in King’s awards It’s not every former prime minister who has two sculpted busts in Ballarat, he might reflect, though no one spoke of it when he came to the shore of Lake Wendouree on Friday. He wasn’t prepared to speak about the current political turmoil for the Liberal-Nationals Coalition in Canberra, either. “I’ll leave those things to the politicians who are still serving,” the former PM said. As to whether he has been asked by his former colleagues for advice about what to do in the emergency, Morrison wasn’t about to break his self-imposed code of silence.



“One of the things I pledge to my colleagues, which I’ve honoured, is that any advice I give them I give to them privately and personally.” He allowed that “it’s a challenging time for all of them, but I really commend Angus for what he had to say on Thursday night [in his budget reply].” A glimpse of the former Liberal politician came through when he added: “I think he [Angus Taylor] set out a very comprehensive alternative to how Australia needs to face the very serious challenges that are ahead of us, and I think that Angus’ invitation to ‘believe again’ was a good one, and it’s certainly one that I share a belief in.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Renovated period homes can offer the best of both worlds: steeped in history and character, and featuring the comfort and efficiency of modern amenities.
